name: The Hall of Values and Names
goal: Store a value under a name, inspect its type, and predict what a name refers to.

description.what: What a value is, how a name gets attached to one, what a type tells you about a value, and why the text a person types in is never a number until you make it one.
description.why: A program that cannot hold on to anything can only ever do one thing and then forget it; a name is how a program remembers, and the type of what it remembers decides what the next line is allowed to do with it.
description.enables: You will be able to store a value under a name, change what that name refers to and predict the result, ask Python what kind of value it is holding, and read a line typed by a person and turn it into a number you can count with.
description.assumes: Only the previous floor: that a program is a list of instructions in a source file, that something runs those instructions from top to bottom, and that `print` shows a value on the screen.
description.assessed: You will predict what programs print, track what a name refers to after each line, and write and repair short programs that read a typed line, store values under names of your choosing, and print the right answer.

sections.title: A value is a single thing the program is holding
sections.body:
Before anything else, a program deals in **values**. A value is one piece of information that exists while the program runs: the whole number `42`, the number-with-a-point `3.5`, the piece of text `gold`, the yes-or-no answer `True`. That is the whole idea, and everything else on this floor is about keeping hold of values and finding out what kind of thing each one is.

When you write a value straight into the source file it is called a **literal** - you have written the thing itself rather than a recipe for working it out. Quotation marks are what tell Python that you mean text: `42` is a number, and `"42"` is a piece of text two characters long that merely looks like one. The quotes are part of the source code, not part of the value, which is why `print("gold")` shows `gold` and not `"gold"`.

A value on its own does nothing and goes nowhere. If a line works out a value and the program neither shows it nor keeps it, that value is gone the instant the line finishes and the program is no better off for having made it. `print` is the first of the two things you can do with a value - show it. Keeping it is the next section, and it is the more important half.

One mechanical detail worth having straight away: a single `print` can take several values separated by commas, and it puts them on one line with a single space between each. Two values in one `print` is one line of output, not two.
sections.code:
print(42)
print(3.5)
print("gold")
print(True)
print(42, 3.5, "gold", True)

annotations.text: `42` with no quotes is a whole number. Python calls this kind of value an int, and it is the kind you count with.
The quotes are an instruction to Python, not part of the value. What appears on screen is `gold` - four characters, no quotes.
`True` is a value in its own right, spelled with a capital T and no quotes. It is not the text `"True"`, although printing them looks identical - a trap this floor returns to.
Four values, one `print`, one line of output, single spaces between them. Commas do not make new lines.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
checkpoint.explain: The tempting answer is that the quoted one shows up differently - it does not, because `print` shows what a value looks like, and the number seven and the one-character text both look like `7`. The difference between them is real and will bite in section four, but you cannot see it in the output, which is exactly why Python gives you a way to ask.

sections.title: A name is a label you attach to a value
sections.body:
A **variable** is a name attached to a value. You attach it with `=`, which is called **assignment**: Python works out whatever is on the right-hand side first, then makes the name on the left refer to that result. From then on, writing the name anywhere gives you back the value.

`=` is not the equals sign of school mathematics, and reading it that way is the commonest beginner error there is. `gold = gold + 5` is not a claim that can be true or false; it is an instruction with two halves in a fixed order. Work out `gold + 5` from whatever `gold` refers to right now, then point `gold` at the answer. As an equation it has no solution at all. As an instruction it is perfectly ordinary.

Assigning to a name that already exists is **rebinding**, and the picture to hold is a luggage label rather than a box. The value is not edited and does not move; the label comes off and goes onto a different value. It follows that if two names were attached to the same value and you rebind one of them, the other is untouched - it never knew about the first name at all.

`gold --> 10`
`gold --> 15     treasure --> 15`
`gold --> 0      treasure --> 15`

Names have rules, and they have judgement. The **rules**: a name may contain letters, digits and underscores, may not begin with a digit, may not contain a space, and may not be one of the words Python has reserved for itself such as `if`, `class` or `for`. `Gold` and `gold` are two different names, because case matters. The **judgement**: a name is written once and read many times, and its job is to tell the next reader what the value means. `total_pence` earns its length; `x`, `tp` and `data` do not, and nor does a name that stopped being true three lines ago.
sections.code:
gold = 10
print(gold)
gold = gold + 5
print(gold)
treasure = gold
gold = 0
print(gold)
print(treasure)

annotations.text: The value 10 is made first, then the name `gold` is attached to it. Nothing existed under that name before this line ran.
Right-hand side first: `gold + 5` is 15, and only then does the label move onto 15. Reading this as an equation is what makes it look impossible.
Two labels, one value. Nothing has been copied here - `treasure` is attached to the very same 15 that `gold` is.
This moves `gold` onto 0. It does not touch the 15, and `treasure` is still attached to it, which is why the last two lines disagree.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? Write both lines.
checkpoint.code:
a = 2
b = a
a = 9
print(a)
print(b)
checkpoint.explain: The tempting answer is `9` twice, on the belief that `b = a` tied the two names together for good. It did not: it attached `b` to whatever value `a` referred to at that instant, which was 2, and the third line then moved only the label `a`. Assignment happens once, when its line runs, and never again.

sections.title: Types: what kind of thing is this, and what may I do with it
sections.body:
Every value has a **type**, which is Python's answer to two questions at once: what kind of thing is this, and what is this allowed to do. Four types cover nearly everything you meet at first.

- `int` - a whole number, such as `12`, `0` or `-4`. What you count with.
- `float` - a number with a decimal point, such as `2.5`. Printing one always shows the point, so a float that happens to be six prints as `6.0`.
- `str` - a piece of text, written in quotes. Short for string, because it is a string of characters.
- `bool` - `True` or `False`, and nothing else. Named after George Boole.

The type decides what an operation means, and one symbol can mean two entirely different things. `*` between two numbers multiplies them, so `12 * 2` is `24`. `*` between text and a whole number repeats the text, so `"lantern" * 2` is `"lanternlantern"`. Python is not guessing what you meant; it is looking at the types and doing the single thing that is defined for them.

`type(value)` asks Python what kind of value it is holding, and printing the result shows something like `<class 'int'>`. Read that as "this is an int" and ignore the word `class` for now - it is a word this dungeon comes back to a long way from here. `type` is a diagnostic tool, and you will reach for it constantly over the next few floors, because when a program does something you did not expect, the cause is very often a value that is not the kind you assumed.
sections.code:
count = 12
price = 2.5
name = "lantern"
sold = True
print(type(count))
print(type(price))
print(type(name))
print(type(sold))
print(name * 2)
print(count * 2)

annotations.text: The decimal point is what makes this a float rather than an int. `2.5` and `2` are different types even though both are numbers.
`type(count)` neither changes `count` nor prints anything by itself - it hands back a value describing the kind, which the surrounding `print` then shows.
Text times a whole number repeats the text. The same `*` as the next line, an entirely different meaning, chosen by the types of the two values.
Number times number multiplies. If you ever cannot predict which of these two behaviours you will get, that is the moment to print the type.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? Write all four lines.
checkpoint.code:
answer = "12"
count = 12
print(type(answer))
print(type(count))
print(answer * 2)
print(count * 2)
checkpoint.explain: The tempting answer for the third line is `24`, because `"12"` looks like a number to a human reader. It is not one - the quotes made it text, and `*` on text repeats it. The two values print identically when shown on their own, so the type is the only thing that tells you what the next line will do with them.

sections.title: input() always hands back text, and that is the first real trap
sections.body:
`input()` stops the program, waits for a person to type a line and press return, and hands that line back as a value. The crucial fact, and it catches everybody once: what it hands back is **always** a `str`. Always. If the person types `12` you receive the two-character text `"12"`, not the number twelve. Python has no way to know whether those characters were meant as a number, a house number or a password, so it does not guess.

This is worse than an ordinary mistake, because half the time it does not look like one. `"12" + "12"` is not an error; it is `"1212"`, because `+` on text joins the two pieces end to end. A program that adds two typed numbers and prints `1212` has not crashed and has not complained - it has quietly printed a wrong answer, and only you can notice. The other half of the time, as with `"12" + 3`, you get an error instead, and an error is honestly the kinder outcome of the two.

The repair is **conversion**. `int(text)` builds a new whole number from text that spells one, and `float(text)` builds a new number-with-a-point. Note **builds a new value**: the original text is not altered by either, exactly as `type` altered nothing. So the standard shape for reading a number is `count = int(input())`, read from the inside outwards - `input()` produces text, `int` turns that text into a number, and the name is attached to the number.

Conversion is not magic and will refuse what it cannot honestly do. `int("3.5")` fails, because `3.5` is not how a whole number is spelled, and `int("twelve")` fails for a more obvious reason. What that refusal looks like on screen, and how to read it, is a floor of its own further down.
sections.code:
typed = "12"
print(type(typed))
print(typed + typed)
count = int(typed)
print(type(count))
print(count + count)

annotations.text: This stands in for `input()`, which cannot wait for typing on a page like this one. Assume somebody has just typed 12 - what you receive is exactly this: text.
`+` on two pieces of text joins them. No error, no warning, and a plainly wrong answer if you believed you were adding numbers.
`int` reads the text and builds a brand new int from it. `typed` is untouched and still refers to the text `"12"`.
The same `+` on two ints adds them. Only the types of the values differ between here and line 3, and they change everything.

checkpoint.prompt: Write a program that reads one line, which will always be a whole number, and prints that number doubled. For the typed line `7` it prints `14`.
checkpoint.starterCode: # read the line, turn it into a number, then print twice it
checkpoint.hint: `input()` gives you text. Something has to turn that text into a number before you can double it.
checkpoint.explain: Doubling the text instead of the number gives `77`, which is the trap in miniature: the program runs, prints something, and is wrong. Converting first is what makes `* 2` mean multiply rather than repeat.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
guided-practice.code:
lamp = "on"
print(lamp)
lamp = "off"
print(lamp)
print(lamp, lamp)
guided-practice.explain: A name gives back whatever it refers to at the moment the line runs, so the same `print(lamp)` written twice can print two different things. If you expected `on` on the second line you were treating the first assignment as a permanent definition rather than as one instruction among several.
guided-practice.hint: Read top to bottom and write down what `lamp` refers to after each assignment.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the two blanks so that this program prints `9` on the first line and `<class 'int'>` on the second.
guided-practice.explain: The first blank has to build a number, because `+ 1` on text is an error rather than nine. The second blank reports a kind rather than producing one, which is the difference between the two: one converts, the other only tells you. Neither changes `raw`, which still refers to the text `"8"` at the end.
guided-practice.hint: One of the two builds a new value; the other only answers a question about a value.

guided-practice.prompt: Give the value `coins` refers to after each line of this program runs.
guided-practice.code:
coins = 3
coins = coins + coins
coins = coins * 10
guided-practice.explain: A name appearing on both sides of `=` is read on the right before it is written on the left, so `coins + coins` is worked out from the old value and the label then moves to the answer. Writing the running value beside each line is the cheapest debugging method there is, and it keeps working on programs far longer than this one.
guided-practice.hint: Work out the right-hand side using the previous line's value, then write down the new one.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a program that reads two lines - a person's name, then the town they live in - and prints one line: the name, then `lives in`, then the town, separated by single spaces. For the typed lines `Ada` and `Bath` it prints `Ada lives in Bath`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
name = input()
# store the second typed line under a name of your own,
# then print the sentence on a single line
guided-practice.solution:
name = input()
town = input()
print(name, "lives in", town)
guided-practice.hint: Each `input()` takes the next line typed, in order. A single `print` can take several values separated by commas, and puts one space between each.
guided-practice.explain: The third test is the interesting one: `Mary Ann` is a single typed line and arrives whole, spaces included, because `input()` reads lines rather than words. Joining with commas inside one `print` gets the single spaces for free, whereas gluing the pieces with `+` would give `Adalives inBath` unless you added the spaces by hand.

guided-practice.prompt: This program should read a whole number and print three more than it, so for the typed line `7` it prints `10`. Instead it stops with an error. Repair it.
guided-practice.hint: Ask what type `price` refers to after the first line, and what `+` can do between that type and a whole number.
guided-practice.explain: Python refuses to join text to a number, which is why this one shouts instead of printing rubbish - `"7" + 3` has no defined meaning, unlike `"7" + "3"`. The negative test matters because it proves the fix converts the text rather than chopping a character off the front of it.

guided-practice.prompt: Put these three lines into the only order that runs without error and prints double the typed number.
guided-practice.explain: A name has to be attached to a value before any line can read it, so each of these lines depends on the one above and no other arrangement survives. Only two orders are even tempting, and the wrong one fails on the very first line because `doubled` does not exist yet.
guided-practice.hint: Which of these three lines mentions a name that no earlier line has attached to anything?

independent-practice.prompt: A market stall sells one kind of goods at a time. Your program reads three typed lines: what the goods are called, the price of one of them in whole pence, and how many were sold. It then prints a single line holding the name, the word `total`, and what the sales came to in pence, separated by single spaces. For the typed lines `lantern`, `40` and `3` it prints `lantern total 120`.
independent-practice.solution:
name = input()
price = int(input())
sold = int(input())
print(name, "total", price * sold)
independent-practice.explain: The three typed lines are not alike and must not be treated alike: one of them is wanted as text and the other two are wanted as numbers, and only you know which is which. A version that leaves all three as they arrive prints something like `lantern total 404040`, which is the free-of-charge lesson that a program printing an answer is not the same as a program printing the right answer.

independent-practice.prompt: Write a program that reads one typed line, prints it back exactly as it arrived, and then on a second line reports what kind of value Python is holding it in. For the typed line `hello` it prints `hello` and then `<class 'str'>`.
independent-practice.explain: All three tests give the same second line, and that is the whole point of the exercise: what was typed makes no difference to the answer, because the kind of value is decided by where it came from rather than by what it looks like. If you expected `<class 'int'>` for the second test, that expectation is the bug this floor exists to remove.

independent-practice.prompt: This program should read two typed lines and print them back in the opposite order to the one they arrived in, so for the typed lines `a` and `b` it prints `b` and then `a`. Instead it prints `b` twice. Repair it.
independent-practice.starterCode:
first = input()
second = input()
first = second
second = first
print(first)
print(second)
independent-practice.solution:
first = input()
second = input()
keep = first
first = second
second = keep
print(first)
print(second)
independent-practice.explain: The third line moves the label `first` onto the second value, and at that instant nothing at all refers to the first value any more - so the fourth line, which looks like it puts things back, only reads the value that is already there. The third test is the one that would let a broken repair through unnoticed, since when both lines are identical every wrong answer looks right.

independent-practice.prompt:
A colleague hands you this working program, which counts jars in a delivery of boxes:

`a = 6`
`b = 3`
`c = a * b`
`print(c)`

There are six boxes and each box holds three jars. Say what each of the three names is holding, give each one a better name and say why yours is better, and explain what a later reader of this program loses when a name is a single letter.
independent-practice.explain: The program is correct today, so the cost of the naming is not a wrong answer - it is that nobody, including you next month, can tell whether it is still correct without being told what the numbers meant. Names such as `boxes`, `jars_per_box` and `total_jars` put that knowledge inside the program, where it cannot be lost, and they also make a mistake visible: `boxes * jars_per_box` obviously reads as a count of jars, whereas `a * b` reads as nothing at all.

choices: `str`, every single time, whatever was typed
whichever of `int`, `float` or `str` the typed characters look most like
no type at all until it is stored under a name
exam.explain: The third option is the tempting one because it is what a helpful language might plausibly do, and some languages do try. Python does not guess: it hands back the characters that were typed, and deciding what they mean is your job, which is why `int(...)` and `float(...)` exist.

exam.prompt: Which of these are legal Python names? Select every one that is.
exam.explain: Digits are fine inside a name and illegal at the front, which is why `chest2` passes and `2nd_chest` does not - Python starts reading a number the moment it sees a leading digit. A space always ends a name, so `chest total` is read as two things rather than one, and a leading underscore is perfectly legal even though it carries a convention you have not met yet.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write both lines.
exam.code:
n = 4
n = n * n
n = n - 6
print(n)
print(type(n))
exam.explain: Each line replaces what `n` refers to using what it referred to a moment earlier, so the answer depends on the order of the lines and nothing else. The second printed line is worth noticing: whole numbers stay whole under multiplication and subtraction, so no decimal point appears from nowhere.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write both lines.
exam.explain: One symbol, two meanings, chosen entirely by the type of the value on the left: repeat for text, multiply for numbers. If both lines looked like they should print `9` to you, the quotes on the first line are doing more work than they appear to.

exam.prompt: Fill the two blanks so this program prints `6` on the first line and `<class 'int'>` on the second.
exam.explain: The second blank is the one that catches people: asking about `size` would report `<class 'str'>`, because converting built a new value under a new name and left the original text exactly as it was. Conversion never edits anything in place.

exam.prompt: Put these three lines into the only order that runs without error and prints double the typed number.
exam.explain: Each line reads a name that only the line above it creates, so the order is forced. Splitting the reading from the converting like this is often clearer than nesting them, and it also gives you somewhere to print the type when a program surprises you.

exam.prompt: Give the value each name refers to at the three points asked for.
exam.code:
x = 5
y = x
x = x + 1
y = y + x
exam.explain: The trap is the last step: `y` still refers to 5 while `x` has moved on to 6, so the sum is 11 rather than the 10 or 12 you get by assuming the two names rise together. `y = x` copied a label at one instant; it did not tie the names to one another.

exam.prompt: Write a program that reads one typed line holding a price such as `2.5`, and prints that price doubled. For the typed line `2.5` it prints `5.0`, and for the typed line `3` it prints `6.0`.
exam.explain: The last test is the one that decides between the two converters: turning `3` into a whole number would print `6` and fail, because the stated answer is `6.0`. A number-with-a-point always prints its point even when nothing follows it, which is Python telling you the type rather than being fussy about the arithmetic.

exam.prompt: This program should read a whole number of grams and print twice that many, so for the typed line `7` it prints `14`. It runs without any error at all and prints `77`. Repair it.
exam.explain: This is the nastier sibling of a program that crashes: `*` is defined between text and a whole number, so Python happily repeats the characters and reports no problem whatsoever. The `0` test is the one that hides it, since repeating `0` twice and doubling zero both look wrong in the same harmless way - which is why an edge case alone never proves a fix.

exam.prompt:
A program reads two typed lines and prints them added together:

`a = input()`
`b = input()`
`print(a + b)`

Somebody types `6` and then `6`, and the program prints `66` without any error. Explain why that happens rather than `12`, and say precisely what you would change to get `12`.
exam.explain: The absence of an error is the important half of this question: `+` is perfectly well defined between two pieces of text, so nothing has gone wrong from Python's point of view and only the person reading the output can tell that the answer is nonsense. Converting each line as it is read, rather than trying to repair the result afterwards, is the fix, because `"66"` no longer contains the information that there were two sixes.
